scenes.say: Week two. Market research and consumer insights, with Estelle Gohil from Fiftyfive5.
scenes.title: Market research and consumer insights
scenes.speaker: Estelle Gohil

scenes.say: Behavioural data tells you what happened. Qualitative research tells you why. And the why decides what the business does next.

verdict.text: The *why* decides what the business does.

scenes.say: Say is not do. A shopper says, I want something cheaper. Keep asking why, and the real driver might be value, convenience, or saving time.
Research drives growth three ways. Identify where to play. Execute, through positioning, pricing and creative. Then evaluate performance.

steps.sub: Where to play: segments, demand, sizing

scenes.say: The toolkit has two modes. Talking: discussion groups, consumer juries, cognitive interviews. And watching: shopping safaris, or body cameras on baristas.
Gen AI helps, but it can't close three gaps. Human and cultural understanding. Data that doesn't exist yet. And the analysis itself. Keep a human in the lead.
scenes.kicker: AI is a tool, not a replacement
scenes.title: Three gaps gen AI *cannot* close

items.head: Data that does not exist yet
The analysis itself
items.sub: Human in the lead, human in the loop

scenes.say: The takeaway? Understand people, don't just collect data. An insight only counts when it enables a decision.

lines.text: An insight only counts when it enables a *decision*.

scenes.say: Week seven. Strategy in a creative agency, with Tim Collier from Cummins and Partners.
scenes.title: Strategy in a creative agency
scenes.speaker: Tim Collier

scenes.say: The planner sits in the middle. The client has a business problem. Strategy asks how it affects the audience. Creative makes something people remember.

steps.sub: How does it affect the audience?

scenes.say: A client hands you a five page brief with everything in it. Your first job is subtraction: get it down to one line a creative team can use.

scenes.title: The 5Cs
scenes.say: To discover, use the five C's. Company, culture, category, connections, and consumer.
Frame it with get, who, to, by. And remember, the single minded proposition is an invitation, not a claim.

lines.text: The single-minded proposition is an *invitation*, not a claim.

scenes.say: The strategist's four steps: discover, synthesise, plan, instruct. And the Effie is the award that proves the work drove profit.
His advice? Be curious, and be opinionated. The world changes a lot. People don't.

lines.text: The world changes a lot. *People don’t.*

scenes.say: Week eight. Creating advertising that works, with Andrew Baxter, after twenty six years running agencies.
scenes.title: Creating advertising that works
scenes.speaker: Andrew Baxter

scenes.title: The right…
scenes.say: Advertising is simple. The right message, to the right person, in the right place, at the right time.
It runs in four steps: strategy, the idea, making it, and placing it.
A billboard gets a two second glance, so use fifteen words or fewer. One message per ad, like Kraft's hunger blaster.
The funnel runs from awareness, to knowledge, liking, preference, conviction, and purchase. Reach about sixty five percent, at least three times.

scenes.kicker: What the most effective advertising is
scenes.say: The best ads are famous and emotional. John Lewis's Monty the Penguin returned eight to one.

scenes.title: Differentiation comes *first*
scenes.say: And differentiation is the most important brand driver, ahead of relevance, esteem and knowledge. A successful campaign now averages ten channels, measured by mix modelling.
And about ninety five percent of purchases are intuitive. We buy, then post-rationalise. Create famous work that works.
Week nine. Creativity, the last remaining commercial superpower, with creative director Brendan Willenberg.
scenes.title: Creativity: the last remaining commercial superpower
scenes.speaker: Brendan Willenberg

scenes.say: Commercial creativity is cheating. Same inputs as everyone else, but an unfair business advantage. And it's a method, not a gift.

lines.text: Creativity is a *method*, not a gift.

scenes.say: Step one is solving the real problem. Go from the brief, past the expected response, to the real problem, then the solution.

scenes.kicker: Extra gum · the Bad Breath Index
scenes.say: Extra's problem: shoppers don't notice gum at the checkout, because they're on their phones. So the Bad Breath Index put a gum prompt into the checkout itself.

scenes.title: Creativity thrives on *constraint*
scenes.say: Creativity thrives on constraint. Rexona couldn't buy media, so it earned it with Pitvertising. And V called out the whole energy drink category instead of copying Red Bull.

items.head: V Energy
items.sub: Can’t out-Red Bull Red Bull, so call out the category.

scenes.say: AI can speed-run the process. But on its own it gives similar, cheap ideas. Use it as your antagonist, not your assistant.
The takeaway? Be simple, not just smart. It's not creative if it's not commercial.

lines.text: It’s not creative if it’s not *commercial*.

scenes.say: Week ten. Inside the world of influencer marketing, with Bryce Coombe from Hypetap.
scenes.title: Inside the world of influencer marketing
scenes.speaker: Bryce Coombe

scenes.say: Australians spend twenty nine and a half hours a month on TikTok. And eighty percent are there mainly for creator content.

stats.label: a month on TikTok, per Australian user

scenes.title: I expect it. I trust it. I buy on it.
scenes.say: Seventy five percent have acted on something they saw in their feed. And social is now search: nearly half of US consumers use TikTok as a search engine.

items.head: 75% have acted on a product in their feed
Social is now *search*
items.sub: ~50% of US consumers search on TikTok; AI models learn from creators

scenes.say: A creator showing the product in real life, like a recipe, gets positive sentiment. Strict brand scripts get neutral at best.

beats.text: Here’s what I actually *cook* with it.

scenes.title: The brand is *liable*, not the influencer
scenes.say: And the brand is liable, not the influencer. A free product counts as paid, so disclose it. And never trust a screen grab.
Views and engagement explain attention, not growth. Measure mental availability, share of voice, perception, and behaviour change.

scenes.title: One demographic does not fit all
scenes.say: Know your brand's eye level. A leader brand uses experts. An eye to eye brand uses creators who are just like you. A subservient brand does the work for people.
The takeaway? Treat influencer as a specialist discipline, and measure growth.
Week eleven. Inside a media agency, with Ali Coysh from Initiative and Geoff Clarke from I.P.G. Mediabrands.
scenes.title: Inside a media agency: strategy, automation and AI
scenes.speaker: Ali Coysh & Geoff Clarke

scenes.say: Media used to mean planning and buying paid space. Now it orchestrates whole customer experiences, across owned, earned, shared and paid.
Ali's logic flow runs from the journey stage, to the bond or barrier, to media role, channel, platform, and environment.
For NRMA in Queensland, that meant the highest non-customer consideration in six years, and a four hundred and sixty seven million dollar commitment to fix the Bruce Highway.

stats.label: committed to fix the Bruce Highway

scenes.kicker: Geoff · bots are an invisible police force
scenes.say: Geoff's point: seventy percent of agency work is downstream, and still manual. Bots now handle setup, tracking and makegoods, saving two hundred and seven thousand hours.

scenes.title: What sets people apart
scenes.say: So the skills that matter are data driven thinking, creative and strategic thinking, and adaptability, with lifelong learning.
The takeaway? It's creative and media now. The lasting differentiator is the craft of your people.

lines.text: The lasting differentiator: the *craft* of your people.

scenes.say: Week twelve. Measuring what matters, with Nicky Barton from Mutinex.
scenes.title: Measuring what matters
scenes.speaker: Nicky Barton

scenes.say: Last-click attribution gives the final click all the credit. It's like a group assignment where whoever hits submit gets the whole mark.

scenes.kicker: Crediting only the bottom of the funnel
scenes.say: Crediting only the bottom of the funnel starves the brand. Then privacy changes broke individual tracking. Ask every platform what it sold, and the answers add up to more than a hundred percent.

lines.text: Crediting only the last touch *starves the brand*.
Then Safari limits, GDPR and Apple’s “ask app not to track” broke individual tracking.
Ask every platform what it sold: the answers add up to *more than 100%*.

scenes.say: Marketing mix modelling reads the whole market: sales, spend, price, seasonality and competitors. It shows what drove sales, and where the next dollar should go.

steps.sub: Sales, spend, price, season, economy, competitors
What drove sales, ROI, the next dollar

scenes.say: It thinks in pictures. A café on a busy corner is your baseline. A song stuck in your head: ads keep working. And the fifth slice of pizza: diminishing returns.
Across eighty three brands, those that kept their brand muscle grew most. If you can't add budget, don't add channels.

lines.text: Brands that kept their *brand muscle* grew most.

scenes.say: The takeaway? Judgement becomes the job. Always ask: how do we know it worked?

lines.text: Always ask: *how do we know it worked?*

scenes.say: Week thirteen. What the final exam looks like.
scenes.title: What the exam looks like
scenes.speaker: Unit coordinator Q&A
scenes.org: Plus Teresa’s email to the class

scenes.say: Five short scenario questions, worth six marks each. Thirty marks in total, all on the guest lectures.

scenes.title: Monday 23 November, 1pm
scenes.say: It's Monday the twenty third of November at one p.m. Check your own venue. Bring your phone for the passcode, and a laptop with Respondus lockdown installed. Do the practice test first.

items.head: Check your own venue
items.sub: Timetable and the exams office email (look in junk)

scenes.say: Transfer is the big skill. A concept shown with Telstra might be asked about Qantas. Know the concept, not just the example.
Aim for three to four hundred words an answer, and answer every part. Concepts are tested. Dates and career paths are not.

Read the question carefully. Why did X do this wants the speaker's reasoning. Could Y do it too wants your own justified view. And model questions want the model applied accurately, tied to the outcome.

verdict.text: Models: apply them accurately, tied to the *outcome*.

scenes.say: Revise every lecture, plus the workshop questions. Good luck.

lines.text: Revise every lecture and the *workshop questions*.

scenes.foot: Exam prep hub and notes below

scenes.say: Week three. What are brands, and why do they matter? With Justin Papps from Tenet.
scenes.title: What are brands and why do they matter?
scenes.speaker: Justin Papps

scenes.say: Start with his definition. A brand is a collection of beliefs and perceptions that create a positive predisposition at the point of choice. It lives in the customer's head.

lines.text: A brand is a collection of *beliefs and perceptions* that create a positive predisposition at the *point of choice*.
It lives in the customer’s head, not in your brand guidelines.

scenes.title: Brand exposures per day
scenes.say: Why does it matter now? In the seventeen hundreds we saw maybe twenty brands a day. Today it's up to ten thousand, and our brains haven't grown.
Brands are economic engines. A Louis Vuitton backpack costs fifty six hundred dollars, fifteen times a rival that beats it on features. Brands equal margin equal power.
They're also behavioural shortcuts. About ninety five percent of thinking is System One: fast and automatic. That's where brand building should aim.

scenes.title: Four pillars, and one paradox
scenes.say: Land four pillars: relevance, distinctiveness, consistency and availability. And the D.B.A. paradox: sonic cues are rarely used, but they're the most effective asset.
His closing line. Attention is cheap. Memory is expensive. Preference is priceless.
Week four. Managing brands with creativity and humanity, with former Telstra C.M.O. Brent Smart.
scenes.title: Managing brands with creativity and humanity
scenes.speaker: Brent Smart

scenes.say: Marketing is a battle for memory. So job one is making the brand memorable, and the biggest risk is taking no risk.

lines.text: The biggest risk is taking *no risk*.

scenes.title: Creative work vs the average ad
scenes.say: And creativity pays. Against the average ad, creative work returns two and a half times the revenue growth, and four times the profit.
When Telstra asked people to draw how the brand felt, they drew a bully in a suit. You can argue with a chart. You can't argue with that drawing.
Only about fifteen percent of buyers are in market right now. The other eighty five percent need brand building, so they remember you later.

note.text: Build *future* demand, don’t just convert it.

scenes.kicker: Binet & Field: the long and the short of it
scenes.say: The benchmark is sixty percent brand, forty activation. Telstra was at twenty. His first move was fifty fifty. Marketing R.O.I. rose from six to over ten.
The whistling ad was hated at launch, then got thirty million organic TikTok views. If it's not bold, it's dumb.
Week five. Managing the evolution of brands, with Shannon Wright from Nestlé. Two brands, two paths: KitKat and Allen's.
scenes.title: Managing the evolution of brands
scenes.speaker: Shannon Wright

scenes.title: KitKat stands for *a break*
scenes.say: KitKat stands for a break, and three truths line up. The brand believes breaks are good. Everyone needs a break. And the bar is made to be broken.

scenes.kicker: The most dangerous person in marketing
scenes.say: The most dangerous person in marketing is the bored brand manager, who changes what didn't need changing. Consistency isn't limiting. It's a superpower.

scenes.kicker: The need is unchanged; the tension evolved
scenes.say: For Gen Z, sixty three percent say they need a break, but sixty four percent can't switch off. So the job is the emotional break.

stats.label: of Gen Z say they need a break

scenes.say: A debate about your brand is a jackpot. The argument over how to eat a KitKat drew twenty seven million engagements. Fan the flames.

stats.label: engagements from the *how do you eat it?* debate

note.text: Fan the flames. Don’t shut it down.

scenes.title: Mapping a brand stretch
scenes.say: Allen's wants to be a playground, not a museum. Stretch is mapped from core, to near adjacency, to credible stretch, to the exception.
The takeaway? Consistency, not sameness. Protect your assets. Use them or lose them.
Week six. Managing a brand for social purpose, with Libby Hogson from UNICEF Australia.
scenes.title: Managing a brand for social purpose
scenes.speaker: Libby Hogson

scenes.say: There are over sixty thousand Australian charities. One for every four hundred and thirty nine people. And fewer donors are giving more.

scenes.kicker: The money was in the wrong place
scenes.say: In twenty twenty UNICEF had zero unprompted awareness. Yet about ninety five percent of spend went on conversion, and five percent on awareness. The top of the funnel was empty.

note.text: Optimising a funnel whose *top was empty*.

scenes.say: Top of mind, donation intent is nineteen percent. Only prompted, it's seven. Mental availability nearly triples intent.
So the positioning: UNICEF inspires Australians with the determination it takes to protect every child, no matter what. Then say it again and again.

lines.text: UNICEF inspires Australians with the *determination* it takes to protect every child, no matter what.
Consistency is the place you hold in people’s minds, said again and again.

scenes.say: Then measure the chain. Ad awareness and share of voice drive unprompted awareness, then donation intent, then market share.
The takeaway? Brand building in a charity is brand building. Stay the course, and measure everything.

lines.text: Brand building in a charity *is* brand building.
